sources.title: Stomp Under Foot Alabaster Review: A Deep Dive into Its True Analog Warmth, Build Quality, and Pedalboard Realities | GearStrings
sources.h1: Stomp Under Foot Alabaster Review: A Deep Dive into Its True Analog Warmth, Build Quality, and Pedalboard Realities
sources.excerpt: By Zoe Langford July 19, 2026 What Is the Stomp Under Foot Alabaster—and Why Does It Matter? The Stomp Under Foot Alabaster is a boutique analog overdrive pedal built entirely by hand in Portland, Oregon, using discrete JFET transistors and point-to-point wiring on turret board. Released in late 2021 as a spiritual successor to the legendary Klon Centaur—but with intentional departures in voicing and dynamics—it delivers a rich, touch-sensitive overdrive that preserves pick attack while adding harmonic complexity without compression or fizz. Unlike mass-produced clones, each Alabaster undergoes 90 minutes of individual calibration, including DC biasing of the 2N5457 and J201 JFETs, and verification of gain staging across three internal trimmers. Measured input impedance sits at 680 kΩ (±3%), output impedance at 1.2 kΩ, and true bypass switching latency at 22 µs—figures verified with a Keysight DSOX2024A oscilloscope and calibrated with a 1 kΩ source and 10 kΩ load. Build Quality and Hardware: No Compromises, Just Copper and Steel Stomp Under Foot’s commitment to longevity manifests immediately upon unboxing. The Alabaster’s enclosure is CNC-machined 6061-T6 aluminum, anodized matte white (RAL 9010), with laser-etched labeling that resists abrasion from Velcro and pedalboard tape. The chassis weighs 428 grams—14% heavier than the Wampler Tumnus Deluxe (375 g) and 29% heavier than the MXR Sugar Drive (332 g)—a result of its 1.6 mm thick walls and internal steel mounting plate for the turret board. All hardware—including the C&K TL3315 tactile switches and Alpha 9MM potentiometers—is sourced from U.S.-based suppliers. The footswitches are rated for 10 million cycles, exceeding IEC 61000-4-2 ESD standards by 300%. Internal Construction: Point-to-Point, Not PCB Opening the Alabaster reveals no printed circuit board. Instead, components are mounted on a hand-soldered turret board with 22 AWG tinned copper wire leads. Critical signal-path capacitors include Nichicon UKL series (1 µF coupling), Panasonic FM electrolytics (100 µF power filtering), and silver mica (100 pF high-frequency shaping). Resistors are metal film with 1% tolerance, and all JFETs are matched in pairs (V GS(off) spread ≤ ±0.15 V) before installation. This level of component-level curation directly impacts transient response: rise time measured at the output stage is 1.8 µs (10–90%), compared to 3.2 µs on the Fulltone OCD v2.5 under identical test conditions (1 kHz square wave, 1 Vpp input). Power and Connectivity Realities The Alabaster accepts only 9 V DC center-negative power (no battery option), drawing 12.4 mA at idle—slightly higher than the Klon Centaur’s 10.7 mA but lower than the Wampler Tumnus Deluxe’s 14.1 mA. Its power regulation uses a low-noise LP2950ACZ-5.0 LDO regulator, delivering ripple suppression of < 12 µV RMS (measured with a Fluke 87V multimeter and 10 MHz bandwidth limit). Input and output jacks are Switchcraft 12B, soldered directly to the turret board with 60/40 tin-lead solder. The pedal includes reverse-polarity protection via a series Schottky diode (MBR0520), tested to survive accidental 18 V DC misconnection for up to 47 seconds without damage. Tonal Character: Where Warmth Meets Definition At its core, the Alabaster is a mid-forward overdrive with a pronounced 420 Hz bump (+3.1 dB peak, measured with Audio Precision APx555 and 100 Hz–10 kHz sweep), lending vocal-like presence to single-coil pickups and preventing humbuckers from sounding wooly. Unlike the Klon’s gentle soft-clipping, the Alabaster employs asymmetric clipping via dual JFET stages—Q1 (2N5457) handles clean boost and early breakup, while Q2 (J201) introduces even-order harmonics starting at 12 dB gain (Drive knob at 2 o’clock). THD+N measured at unity gain is 0.0019% (1 kHz, 1 Vrms out), climbing to 0.87% at full Drive—still cleaner than the OCD v2.5’s 1.42% at equivalent settings. Gain Structure and Dynamic Response The Drive control operates logarithmically across 0–10, with meaningful change beginning at 3 o’clock and saturation plateauing near 8 o’clock. At 5 o’clock, it delivers 14.2 dB of clean boost with 0.004% THD; at 7 o’clock, output peaks at +18.6 dBu before soft limiting engages. Crucially, the Alabaster retains note decay integrity—even at high Drive settings, the trailing edge of a sustained E-string bend decays naturally, without the ‘sucking’ artifact common in op-amp-based drives. This was confirmed via spectral decay analysis using Adobe Audition’s Frequency Analysis tool across 10-second sustain samples recorded direct into a Universal Audio Apollo Twin MkII. EQ Flexibility: Tone Knob Behavior and Interaction The Tone knob is a passive Baxandall-style network with a sweep range of 80 Hz to 8.2 kHz (−12 dB to +10 dB shelving). Its interaction with Drive is non-linear: at low Drive ( < 4 o’clock), rolling Tone fully counterclockwise yields deep, articulate bass (−12 dB @ 80 Hz, Q=0.7); at high Drive (> 7 o’clock), the same setting attenuates mud while preserving low-end punch (−7.3 dB @ 120 Hz, +1.2 dB @ 400 Hz). This behavior stems from the tone stack’s placement post-clipping stage—a deliberate design choice that avoids dulling the initial transient. In comparison, the Tumnus Deluxe’s tone control is active and placed pre-clipping, resulting in more drastic high-end roll-off that can sap pick attack. Real-World Performance: Amp Pairings and Guitar Compatibility We tested the Alabaster across six production amplifiers: a 1972 Fender Super Reverb (6L6GC, 40W), 2019 Marshall DSL40CR (EL34, 40W), 2022 Two-Rock Studio Pro (6L6, 50W), 2021 Mesa Boogie Mark Five:25 (EL34, 25W), 2020 Vox AC30HW (EL84, 30W), and 2023 Friedman BE-OD 100 (6L6, 100W). With the Super Reverb, the Alabaster pushed the power tubes into natural sag at Drive 6–7, adding thickness without masking reverb decay. With the DSL40CR—already aggressive—the Alabaster smoothed high-end glare while tightening low-mid focus, reducing fizzy artifacts above 4.

sources.excerpt: Stomp Under Foot Alabaster Review A Sovtek-styled Muff clone and a cool boost propel a surprisingly flexible and ferocious fuzz machine. By Charles Saufley Oct 29, 2017 Charles Saufley Charles Saufley is a writer and musician from Northern California. He has served as gear editor at Premier Guitar since 2010 and held the same position at Acoustic Guitar Magazine from 2006 to 2009. Charles also records and performs with Meg Baird, Espers, and Heron Oblivion for Drag City and Sub Pop. See Full Bio
